name: Mediator
intent: Centralise how a group of objects communicate, so they talk to a mediator instead of to each other.
scenario: People in a chat room send messages. Nobody holds references to other users; the room delivers each message and can apply rules.
problem: If every user keeps references to every other user, adding a user means updating everyone, and the number of connections grows with the square of the group size. Rules like filtering or muting would have to be duplicated in every user.
solution: Introduce a ChatRoom mediator. Users register with the room and send everything through it. The room decides who receives what and is the single place for shared rules. Users know only the room, not each other.
pain: Each user holds references to every other user
Adding a user means updating all existing users
Connections grow quickly: n users, n x (n-1) links
Rules (filtering, muting) are duplicated in every user
benefits: Each user knows only the room
Adding a user is one register() call
Connections stay at n, not n squared
Rules live in the mediator, once
whenToUse: A set of objects communicate in complex, tangled ways
You want to reuse components without dragging their neighbours along
You need one place for the interaction rules: chat rooms, UI dialogs, air traffic control
whenNotToUse: Only two or three objects interact simply
A simple event/observer approach would be enough
The mediator would only forward calls without adding logic
pitfalls: The mediator can grow into a god object that knows everything
Moves complexity rather than removing it: the room can become hard to maintain
A single point of failure and a possible bottleneck
Easy to confuse with Observer: a mediator coordinates, an observer broadcasts

quiz.question: A chat room has 20 users and each user holds a reference to every other user, with one link for each pair. The room grows to 40 users. Compared with routing everything through a room mediator, what is the link count?
options: 380 links between pairs now, compared with 80 links to a mediator
1,560 links between pairs now, compared with 40 links to a mediator
780 links between pairs now, compared with 40 links to a mediator
400 links between pairs now, compared with 40 links to a mediator
quiz.explanation: With one link per pair, n users need n(n-1)/2 links: 780 for 40 users, up from 190 for 20. With a mediator each user has one link, so 40. Direct links grow with the square of the group size.

quiz.question: A dialog has 8 widgets. Each one keeps references to the others and decides on its own to enable or disable them. Adding a 9th widget means editing 5 other classes. What is the best fix?
options: Create a common base widget class that holds the enable and disable rules for all widgets
Store all the widgets in a static global list and let each widget scan it when it changes
Have each widget report to a dialog object that holds the enable and disable rules in one place
Make each widget subscribe to the widgets it depends on, using change events between them
quiz.explanation: A mediator keeps the interaction rules in one class, so a new widget is wired in one place and widgets stay reusable. Widgets that subscribe to each other keep the tangle, only with events. A global list still couples each widget to the others.

quiz.question: A chat room mediator started small. It now has 3,000 lines covering moderation, presence, billing limits and file sharing, and every team edits it. What is the best way to deal with it?
options: Split the rules into focused collaborators, one per concern
Move the rules back into the user classes, so each user decides what it may receive
Make the room a singleton so there is only one copy of the rules to maintain
Replace the mediator with observers, where each user subscribes to all other users
quiz.explanation: A mediator that knows everything is a god object, and the answer is smaller pieces with one concern each. Pushing rules back into users brings back the duplicated rules and many-to-many links. A singleton does not reduce size.
